title: Heat Pump vs Furnace: Think TWICE Before Switching
summary: HVAC contractor compares heat pumps, furnaces and dual fuel using Salt Lake City temperature data and recommends dual fuel for most homes in that climate.

assertions.quote: A heat pump doesn't create heat, it moves heat.
The colder it gets, the less heat there is to pull out of the air, and the less efficient it becomes.
A heat pump puts out air that's typically 85° to 95°.

verdicts.note: Heat pump supply air is typically 90-100°F versus 120-140°F for furnaces, a common comfort complaint.

assertions.quote: They'll also absolutely destroy your electric bill.
That's just an expensive space heater with better marketing.
Run the heat pump when it's cheaper than gas. Switch to the furnace when gas is cheaper than backup strips.

verdicts.note: With a well-set changeover temperature dual fuel can beat either fuel alone, but the saving over gas alone is small where gas is cheap and it needs two systems.

assertions.quote: But from a heat pump running about 300% efficiency, about a dollar 11. Actually slightly cheaper than gas at current rates.
continue to [clears throat] provide heat down to minus 13 or colder.
up to two $2,000 in federal tax credits for qualifying heat pumps

verdicts.note: The IRA's 25C credit gave 30% up to $2,000 for qualifying heat pumps placed in service 2023-2025; the 2025 budget law ended it.

assertions.quote: Geothermal is the most efficient heating and cooling system available. Period. It's also the most expensive to install.

verdicts.note: Ground-source systems reach higher seasonal COPs but loop fields push installed costs to several times an air-source system.

assertions.quote: won't be around long enough for the efficiency savings to pay back the install costs.

verdicts.note: Where gas is cheap the annual saving from switching is small or negative, so the full cost of replacing working equipment seldom pays back.
Even assuming replacement at end of life, switching from natural gas to a heat pump rarely produces a private benefit, almost never in cold climates; replacing a working furnace would only add cost.

In RMI's four-city model at 2018 prices, homes with gas heat that only need a new furnace usually pay more over 15 years to electrify than to stay on gas, even when the furnace is being replaced anyway (an advocacy model of a few cities).

In the UK the switch from a gas boiler has a net private cost of about £4,121 over 20 years even after the £7,500 grant, because running costs are higher on a standard tariff, so energy savings never repay the purchase (UK boilers; time-of-use tariffs change this).

assertions.quote: If you've got solar panels, the math gets even better.

verdicts.note: Solar lowers the effective electricity price, but winter heating demand peaks when solar output is lowest, so the gain depends on net metering terms.
